newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ING under pressure over accounting policy.
newsitem.headline: ING under pressure over accounting policy.

text.p: Dutch financial services giant Internationale Nederlanden Groep NV is resisting pressure to change an accounting policy which has been depressing earnings.

Analysts said they wanted the banking and insurance group to move into line with other major Dutch financial services groups by including unrealised capital gains on its equity and property investment portfolio in the profit and loss account.
But ING said it had no plans to depart from its conservative practice of taking these movements only through its balance sheet while Aad Jacobs remained as executive board chairman.
"It's not on the agenda here. We have a very conservative approach," ING spokesman Ruud Polet told Reuters.
BZW Nederland analyst Heinie Hakker said he would welcome the inclusion of indirect returns on investments in profits, similar to Aegon and Fortis Amev.
Fortis Amev takes all unrealised gains and losses through its profit and loss account while Aegon includes an average indirect return which smoothes out volatile movements.
Hakker said ING could boost profits by some 15 percent if it adopted Aegon's policy. ING's first half 1996 net profit rose 28 percent to 1.51 billion guilders.
"It's a big thing for many investors. Ultimately they will have to move to a system where they do it," he said.

Hakker also called on ING to change its dividend policy, under which it is more attractive to take dividends as stock rather than cash, or launch a share buy-back, to limit the dilution of earnings caused by the creation of new shares.
Ton Gietman of Van Meer James Capel said ING should move in line with its peers as its earnings would be easier to analyse.
"We have been requesting that for two years and they have been rejecting it," he said, adding that this may change when Jacobs retires, possibly in mid-1998.
Gietman said ING traded at a discount to Aegon, which derives a significant part of its profits from unrealised gains on its investments.
He said ING's accounting policy may also encourage its fund managers to invest more for income than capital growth.
Hans Pluijgers of Kempen and Co said ING was trading at about the same multiple as Fortis of 11.6 times 1996 earnings, when it should be higher due to better growth prospects.
He found it strange that a major part of its activities were not included in profits, but ING would have to reveal the size of its indirect returns next year when it lists in New York.

CS First Boston analyst Kishore Banger said it could be argued that while Aegon and Fortis Amev were "reflecting back" some unrealised capital gains to shareholders, ING was understating its earnings.
He said most European insurance companies included such price movements in earnings.
"It would be welcomed by the market if ING did adopt that approach," he said.
But he said analysts made allowance for this in assessing the value of its shares against rival companies.
